NDT training in Anchorage: how it works for Anchorage employers and technicians

Short answer: NDT training for Anchorage technicians is delivered by Atlantis NDT as live online classroom sessions, or onsite at your company's shop, yard or facility, under ASNT Level III oversight. Courses follow ASNT SNT-TC-1A for Level I, II and III in UT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET. Certification is issued by your employer under its written practice once training hours, supervised experience, exams and a vision test are complete. Quotes are on request.

That short answer hides a lot of Alaska-specific detail, so this section goes further. Anchorage is where most of the state's inspection companies keep their offices, calibration benches and training records, even though much of the actual inspection happens hundreds of miles away: on the North Slope, along the Trans-Alaska Pipeline corridor, at the Valdez Marine Terminal, on Cook Inlet platforms and at the Kenai Peninsula refinery and gas facilities. That geography shapes how training works here. Technicians rotate on and off the Slope, crews are small, and pulling five people into a classroom for a week in the Lower 48 is expensive and disruptive. The model that fits Anchorage best is theory delivered live online between rotations, with hands-on practical work and exams run onsite at the employer's facility in Anchorage or at a field location, overseen by a Level III.

Atlantis NDT does not have a training centre in Anchorage or anywhere else, and we will not pretend otherwise. What we do have is a SNT-TC-1A-based curriculum, a Level III lead instructor, a 3D practice simulator, and the ability to bring the course to your people. If you run an Anchorage inspection company, a fabrication shop in the Ship Creek or Midtown industrial areas, or a maintenance department that needs in-house Level II capability, the rest of this page explains exactly how that works. Request an Anchorage training quote and we will reply with cohort and onsite options within one business day.

ASNT Level I, II and III courses available in Anchorage

Every course below is built on the ASNT SNT-TC-1A recommended practice and can be taken at Level I, Level II, or as Level III examination preparation. The table maps each method to the kind of work Anchorage and Alaska employers actually use it for. It is context, not a promise that any particular employer will hire you: the employer's written practice always decides what qualifies.

MethodLevelsWhat Anchorage and Alaska employers use it forPrerequisite
UT (Ultrasonic Testing)I, II, III prepWall-thickness surveys on North Slope process piping and gathering lines, corrosion mapping, weld inspection on pipeline tie-ins and module fabricationLevel I: none beyond employer entry rules; Level II: Level I plus experience per the written practice
PAUT (Phased Array UT)II, III prepGirth-weld and corrosion inspection on pipeline and facility piping where RT is impractical in camp settings; encoded scans for recordsUT Level II (or concurrent) recommended
TOFD (Time of Flight Diffraction)II, III prepThick-wall weld inspection and flaw sizing on vessels, tanks and heavy-wall pipe, often paired with PAUTUT Level II recommended
RT (Radiographic Testing)I, II, III prepPipeline and piping weld radiography, fabrication shop RT, film and digital interpretationRadiation safety qualification is separate and regulated; see the licensing section below
MT (Magnetic Particle Testing)I, II, III prepSurface crack detection on ferritic welds, lifting gear, structural steel and heavy equipment used in cold-weather serviceNone beyond employer entry rules
PT (Liquid Penetrant Testing)I, II, III prepSurface-breaking defects on stainless and non-ferrous parts, aircraft components, valves and machined partsNone beyond employer entry rules
VT (Visual Testing)I, II, III prepWeld visual inspection, tank and structural condition surveys, the first check on almost every Alaska inspection scopeNone beyond employer entry rules
ET (Eddy Current Testing)I, II, III prepAircraft structure and wheel inspection for the Anchorage air-cargo and aviation sector, heat-exchanger tubing, coating thicknessNone beyond employer entry rules

What a UT course covers. Sound physics, transducers and couplants, calibration blocks and reference standards, straight-beam thickness measurement, angle-beam weld inspection, DAC and TCG construction, discontinuity characterisation and reporting. For Alaska crews we spend real time on temperature: how cold steel, frozen couplant and wind-chilled probes shift velocity and signal quality, and why calibration on a block at the same temperature as the part matters.

What a PAUT and TOFD course covers. Focal laws, sectorial and linear scans, encoded scanning, scan plans, TOFD geometry and lateral wave interpretation, dead zones, and data review. These are the methods Alaska operators increasingly specify for pipeline and heavy-wall work because they produce a permanent, auditable record without the exclusion zones RT needs on a crowded pad.

What an RT course covers. Radiographic principles, isotope and X-ray sources, film and digital image quality, IQIs, geometric unsharpness, exposure calculation, and interpretation of weld radiographs. The course teaches the technique; the separate radiation safety training and certification needed to handle sources in the field is regulated federally in Alaska, as explained below.

MT, PT, VT and ET courses cover the physics of each method, equipment and consumables, technique selection, acceptance criteria from the codes your employer works to, and reporting. For Level III candidates, we prepare you for the Basic, Method and Specific examinations with structured review and mock papers. See our ASNT Level III training page for how that programme is organised.

SNT-TC-1A certification path in Anchorage, step by step

SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice, not a licence. Certification is employer-based, which means an Anchorage NDT company certifies its own people against its own written practice. Here is the path in order:

  1. Your employer's written practice. This document sets the training hours, experience hours, exam content and pass marks the company uses for each method and level. If you are a new company in Anchorage without one, that is the first thing to fix; see the Level III services section below.
  2. Formal classroom training. You complete the method-specific classroom hours required by the written practice for your level. Atlantis NDT delivers this live online or onsite. Check the minimums in our training-requirements matrix rather than relying on figures quoted by third parties.
  3. On-the-job experience. You accumulate documented experience in the method under the supervision of a certified individual. For Alaska technicians this is often logged across rotations, so keep a signed log per hitch.
  4. General examination. A written test on the principles and theory of the method.
  5. Specific examination. A written test on the equipment, procedures, codes and acceptance criteria your employer actually uses.
  6. Practical examination. A hands-on test on real specimens with known discontinuities, administered and graded under a Level III.
  7. Vision examination. Near-vision acuity and colour contrast, typically repeated annually.
  8. Certification by the employer. The employer's Level III reviews the file and the company certifies you. The certification is valid for that employer.
  9. Recertification. At the interval set by the written practice, you requalify by evidence of continued satisfactory performance or re-examination.

Our SNT-TC-1A training and certification guide explains each step in more depth, including what happens when you change employers.

Online, live-virtual or onsite NDT training for Anchorage crews

We offer three delivery modes, and Anchorage employers usually mix them.

  • Live online classroom. Instructor-led sessions in real time, with questions, whiteboard walkthroughs and quizzes. This suits technicians on their off rotation who are home in Anchorage, the Mat-Su Valley or the Kenai Peninsula, and it avoids flying crews out of state. See NDT training online for the format.
  • Onsite at your facility. A Level III-overseen programme at your Anchorage shop or a field location, using your equipment and your procedures, with practical sessions on specimens. This is the most efficient option for a company training several people at once. Ask about onsite training for your Anchorage crew.
  • Classroom cohorts. Where enough candidates are ready at the same time, we schedule a dedicated cohort.

Scheduling around Alaska realities. The North Slope and Cook Inlet have their own rhythms: winter ice-road and pad construction seasons, summer maintenance windows when many facility turnarounds and pigging campaigns run, and fixed rotation schedules such as two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off. We plan theory blocks so a technician can complete them across consecutive off-rotations, and we schedule onsite practical sessions for the shoulder periods when your people are in town. Tell us your rotation pattern and your next shutdown window and we will build the plan around it.

Practical exams are never done online. The written general and specific exams can be proctored in the way your written practice allows, but the practical must be performed on real specimens under Level III oversight.

Where NDT technicians work in Anchorage

Anchorage is the office, logistics and training base for an inspection market that stretches across the whole state. The main employer sectors are:

  • North Slope oil production. Prudhoe Bay, Kuparuk, the Colville River and Alpine fields, and newer developments to the west. Operators and their inspection contractors need corrosion monitoring on production piping and flowlines, weld inspection on module and pipeline construction, and integrity work on facility vessels. Much of the module fabrication and inspection planning is organised from Anchorage.
  • The Trans-Alaska Pipeline System. The 800-mile line from Prudhoe Bay to the Valdez Marine Terminal, with its pump stations and tank farm, generates ongoing integrity inspection. Pipeline welding and inspection in the US commonly reference API 1104, and PHMSA federal pipeline safety rules shape operators' integrity programmes.
  • Cook Inlet and the Kenai Peninsula. Offshore platforms, subsea and onshore gas gathering, the Nikiski industrial area and the Kenai refinery all need UT thickness surveys, weld inspection and tank work.
  • Aviation. Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport is one of the world's busiest air-cargo hubs, and Anchorage is home to regional and bush airlines and their maintenance shops. Aircraft NDT relies heavily on ET, PT, UT and VT. Aerospace employers often also work to NAS 410 personnel requirements, which Atlantis does not train to, but the SNT-TC-1A method knowledge is directly relevant.
  • Military. Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson sits on the edge of the city, and defence maintenance and construction contracts bring their own inspection requirements.
  • Port, marine and infrastructure. The Port of Alaska in Anchorage, which handles a large share of the state's inbound freight, is in a long-running modernisation programme; marine terminals, fishing-fleet repair yards, bridges and structural steel all need VT, MT and UT, often under AWS D1.1 for structural welding.
  • Fabrication shops. Anchorage shops build skids, modules, tanks and piping for the oilfields, typically working to ASME Section VIII for vessels, ASME B31.3 for process piping and ASME Section V for NDT technique requirements.

Radiography licensing in Alaska. Alaska is not an NRC Agreement State. That means the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, through its Region IV office, licenses companies that use radioactive sources for industrial radiography in Alaska, and radiographers using those sources must meet the federal certification requirements in 10 CFR Part 34, typically through an NRC-recognised certifying entity. The State of Alaska regulates X-ray equipment. In practice, an Anchorage RT crew needs its employer to hold the appropriate licence, and each radiographer and assistant needs the radiation safety training and certification the licence and federal rules require. Our RT method course does not replace that radiation safety qualification; it teaches the imaging and interpretation skills that sit alongside it. Always confirm current requirements directly with the NRC and your company's radiation safety officer.

What local employers typically ask for. Job postings in the Alaska market usually ask for SNT-TC-1A Level II in UT plus at least one of MT, PT or VT, with PAUT increasingly listed. Many owners also ask their inspectors to hold API 510, 570 or 653 credentials or AWS CWI for specific roles. Atlantis does not offer those programmes; we mention them only so you know what the market looks for. Rotational roles also require site safety orientations and drug and alcohol testing, which are separate from NDT certification. For pay context, see our NDT salary guide.

Level III services and written practices for Anchorage NDT companies

Many Anchorage inspection firms are small: a handful of technicians, one or two Level IIs, and no in-house Level III. Under SNT-TC-1A, the company still needs a written practice, qualified examiners and a Level III to approve procedures and administer exams. Outside Level III services fill that gap.

  • Written practice development. We draft or revise your written practice so it matches the methods you actually perform, the codes your clients specify, and the way you run rotational crews. See NDT written practice development.
  • Procedure writing and review. Method procedures for UT thickness, angle-beam, PAUT, TOFD, MT, PT and VT aligned to ASME, API or AWS requirements your clients reference.
  • Examinations. Level III-administered general, specific and practical exams, and records that stand up in a client audit.
  • Corporate programmes. Structured training plans for a whole crew, scheduled around rotations. See corporate NDT training.

If an owner audit or a new contract is coming up and your certification files are not where they should be, book a Level III consultation. Our SNT-TC-1A guidance page is a good place to start reading first.

Practise before the practical exam

The practical exam is where most candidates feel the pressure. Our Practical NDT 3D simulator lets you practise 12 NDT methods across 5 environments: an NDT lab, a welding workshop, an aircraft hangar, an oil and gas site and a storage tank. For Anchorage technicians the oil and gas site, storage tank and aircraft hangar scenes are the closest to the work you will actually do, and you can rehearse set-up, scanning and interpretation from home between rotations.

Be clear about what the simulator is: practice. It does not replace hands-on time with real equipment and it does not replace the practical examination, which must be performed on real specimens under Level III oversight. Use it to build familiarity so that your hands-on hours are more productive.

Your instructor

Training is led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. He designs the curriculum, oversees onsite programmes, and reviews examination content so that what you learn maps to how SNT-TC-1A certification actually works inside an employer.

Frequently asked questions about NDT training in Anchorage

How do I get NDT certified in Anchorage?

Under SNT-TC-1A, certification comes from your employer. You complete the classroom training and supervised experience required by the employer's written practice, pass general, specific and practical exams under a Level III, pass a vision test, and the employer certifies you. Atlantis NDT provides the training, exam preparation and, for employers who need it, Level III services.

Can I take NDT training online in Alaska?

Yes, the classroom portion can be completed through live online sessions, which suits technicians on rotation. The hands-on practical training and the practical exam need real equipment and specimens, so those are done onsite at your employer's facility or at an arranged location. See online NDT training.

Is there an NDT training centre in Anchorage?

Atlantis NDT does not operate a physical centre in Anchorage. We deliver live online and onsite at your facility, which for most Alaska employers is more practical than flying crews to a centre in the Lower 48.

How long does UT Level 2 training take?

It depends on the minimum classroom and experience hours in your employer's written practice, whether you are starting from Level I, and how your rotations fall. SNT-TC-1A recommends minimums that employers can adopt or raise. Check the figures in our training-requirements matrix and we will build a schedule around your hitches.

Do I need a license for radiography in Alaska?

Radiography with radioactive sources in Alaska is licensed by the NRC because Alaska is not an Agreement State, and radiographers must meet federal certification requirements. X-ray equipment is regulated by the State. Your employer holds the licence and its radiation safety officer will tell you what personal qualification you need. Our RT course covers technique and interpretation, not the regulatory radiation safety qualification.

What does NDT training cost in Anchorage?

We do not publish prices. The quote depends on the method, level, number of candidates, online versus onsite delivery, and whether Level III exam services are included. Request a quote and we respond with cohort and onsite options within one business day.

Is ASNT certification recognised by Anchorage employers?

SNT-TC-1A is the personnel qualification basis most US oil, gas and industrial employers use, and Alaska employers commonly list it in job postings. Remember that SNT-TC-1A certification belongs to the employer that issued it; a new employer can review your records and recertify you under its own written practice.

Which NDT method should I learn first for work on the North Slope?

UT is the method most often requested for corrosion and thickness work, with VT, MT and PT as common companions. PAUT and TOFD are valuable once you have UT Level II. Ask a prospective employer which methods their current contracts need before committing.

Can you train our crew during a Cook Inlet or Slope maintenance window?

We plan theory for off-rotation periods and practical sessions for when your people are in Anchorage, so training does not compete with a turnaround or pigging campaign. Share your schedule and we will propose a plan.

Do you offer API 570 or AWS CWI courses in Anchorage?

No. Atlantis NDT training is ASNT SNT-TC-1A only. Some Alaska employers also ask for API or AWS credentials for particular roles, and you would obtain those through the bodies that issue them.

Can I practise the practical exam from home?

You can rehearse with the Practical NDT simulator, including oil and gas, tank and hangar scenes. It is a practice tool only; your actual practical exam is on real specimens under a Level III.

Where can I find practice questions for UT Level II?

Start with our UT Level 2 practice questions, then use the mock exams provided during your course.
